title: Markets, Efficiency, and Price Signals: Crash Course Economics #19
transcript: Adrian: Hi, I'm Adrian Hill. Jacob: And I'm Jacob Clifford, and this is a crash course in economics. We are going to talk about a lot of things during the day. Adrian: Everything from faltering planned economies to heartless free markets, from price gouging to mechanisms. But it's not all bad news. We are going to learn that price signals indicate that skinny jeans are on their way to disappearing. Opening Music Adrian: We talked about the difference between free market economies, where supply and demand determine what will be created, and planned economies, where government agencies decide what will be created. Today we will expand on this and talk about why competitive markets have been more successful in delivering most of the things people want. Central planning has several advantages. Everyone who wants a job has a job and production is in line with the ideal shared goals of society. But the reality regarding this was much less ideal for consumers in these companies. In the Soviet Union, the central planners concentrated on the production of military equipment and tools . There were shortages of consumer goods, such as soap, sugar, and electronic products. It turns out that people place greater importance on smartphones and good coffee than on tractors. And so countries like China and Cuba moved away from broad central planning. Jacob: The problem with central planning is that it is inefficient. When economists talk about efficiency, they're talking about several types of efficiency that are different from the efficiency you might be familiar with. The first is production efficiency: the idea that products are produced at the minimum possible cost. This means that there is no waste of resources and raw materials and workers and machines are used to their maximum potential. Central planners, in general, are not so focused on price. But in the free market, private business owners have an incentive not to waste because they want to maximize profits. In the words of Milton Friedman; "No one spends someone else's money as carefully as they spend their own." The second type of efficiency is called allocative efficiency, which means that the things we produce are the things that consumers really want. In other words, our limited resources are allocated to things we value. Let 's say a company only produces skinny jeans, then if it doesn't employ too many workers and if it doesn't end production with excess raw materials, then it produces at the lowest possible price which is what constitutes production efficiency. The problem is that it only makes skinny jeans. Even if the company is efficient in production, it is probably inefficient in allocation. Consumers don't just want skinny jeans, some want bootcut jeans. Central planners will probably be less efficient at allocating because they have less information about what people want. Adrian: Consumer product manufacturers in the free market collect a lot of information about consumer preferences through tools like market research. But they can learn a lot about consumer desires by looking at prices. Economists call this price signaling. Let's go to the thought bubble. Okay, so if people pay high prices for skinny jeans, that tells manufacturers, "The company is very interested in skinny jeans, start making them." If no one wants skinny jeans, manufacturers will start making something else instead. Here's another example: Tablets weren't really popular until Apple introduced the iPad. Then, boom! The market exploded. In fact, I know about 11% of you are watching this video on a tablet right now. Because I can see you. And I can't believe you're still wearing skinny jeans. When Google, Samsung, and Microsoft saw that Apple was selling millions of iPads for $500 and up, they had an incentive to enter the market. Price signals not only signal to manufacturers what to produce, they also help distribute tablets to people who value them. For example: If someone's grandmother doesn't really want a tablet and she was only willing to pay $20 for it, she won't get it. Unless the grandchildren drag her into the 21st century by buying it for her for Christmas. Some economists love price signals so much that they argue with the tradition of gift-giving. This argument was popularized by economist Joel Waldfogel, who argued that gift-giving is inefficient. From a macroeconomic perspective, holiday shopping boosts consumer spending, GDP, and employment. But, if too many people buy products that the end consumer doesn't appreciate, then a lot of resources are wasted. Of course, this analysis does not take into account additional benefits of gift giving such as a symbol of love and appreciation between family and friends. But the facts remain: the ideal gift in terms of effectiveness is cash. Money from the heart. Thank you, thought bubble. Theoretically, in a free market, producers cannot improve their situation without improving the situation of consumers. If a company produces too many units of a product or produces an unsolicited product, it will have to adapt quickly, or it will go bankrupt . Competition between businesses keeps prices and quality high. This is the invisible hand of our old friend Adam Smith. It 's important to take a step back here and point out that we are not saying that free markets are always good and that government intervention is always bad. Most economists understand that markets are imperfect and that they often fail to meet society's needs. In these cases, economists encourage the government to create regulation or take direct control of markets to improve social welfare. In the United States, which is often mistakenly considered a free-market economy, it turns out that almost everything is regulated. For example, the FDA does not approve any wheat that contains nine milligrams or more of rodent excrement per kilogram. And the government directly controls the markets for national defense and public education. The field of public economics notices these things. Now, I love rodent droppings and public education like the girl next door, but let's get back to markets and the role of prices in determining how we use our limited resources. So price signals help us use our resources efficiently, but that doesn't mean everyone agrees that it's always right or fair. Take the price gouging. Price gouging occurs when sellers raise prices for necessities such as food, water, or fuel. While there is something like an emergency. Some argue that this method exploits consumers and is an example of the cruelty of the markets. In the United States, anti-price gouging laws exist in 34 states. But many economists say these laws encourage inefficiency and actually make the problem worse. They argue that letting prices rise during a crisis encourages others, outside the disaster area, to come in and sell essential goods. If there is no way to raise prices, then there is less incentive to bring those goods in. What’s more, high prices for things like batteries, sleeping bags, and generators mean that people who don’t really need them won’t buy them, making them more available to people who do. It’s not always government laws that limit price gouging. It may be the desire to make a profit that keeps prices low. It’s clear that businesses can make a lot of money in the short term from price gouging, but what happens in the long term? Consumers will remember how they were treated. That’s part of the reason why some businesses like Walmart have an emergency operations center and a forecaster they employ to predict weather trends. It helps them hold Products like water and batteries in stock when they are needed. Not only is this profitable, it is also good for public relations. In fact, in some cases, such as Hurricane Katrina in 2005, private businesses responded faster than government agencies. Another example of how a pricing system is perceived as unfair is charging prices below cost. This is called predatory pricing. It is the idea that a business can drive competitors out of business by charging low prices even at the cost of short-term losses . Competitors who cannot afford to keep prices that low will have to go out of business, giving those who remain market share and the ability to raise prices. Let's talk about Walmart again. Walmart has been sued dozens of times for predatory pricing. Their size allows them to pressure distributors and sell products at very low prices. Although many consumers like these low prices, it is bad for competitors. Especially for small, privately owned stores, which are sometimes forced out of business. But is this predatory pricing? In the United States, The courts said no. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) website claims, "Although the FTC has examined the predatory pricing claims in depth, the courts, including the Supreme Court, have not accepted these claims." So predatory pricing lawsuits are common, but they rarely succeed in the U.S. In Germany, Walmart faced similar allegations in 2000 and was ordered to raise some of its prices. The company ended up leaving Germany in 2006. Predatory pricing is tricky and dangerous. When businesses are able to outbid their competitors by selling products at a loss, they will eventually have to raise prices above market prices to recoup those losses. In the short term, consumers will have to pay more. But eventually, other businesses will see the high prices and enter the market. The end result is that there is no certainty that predatory pricing is profitable in the long run. Jacob: There are plenty of examples of corporate greed, inequality, and environmental neglect that make people think that markets are evil. And they are. Thanks for watching! See you next week! [Ending music] Wait, but there are also examples of socially conscious companies. That make an effort to protect the environment and help with the causes of cultivation. Capitalism, with its emphasis on price rather than fairness, is often described as the opposite of altruism . But the two can, and do, coexist. But here's the big deal: Capitalism, with its system of price signals, is simply crowdfunding. We collectively choose what we want and how we want it to be when we spend our money. After all, companies can't force you to buy their stuff; they have to earn your money. So if you want to see real change in the world, don't just complain about corporations being greedy; expect more from them. We also need to expect more from ourselves. If you don't agree with the way a chain treats its employees, then don't shop there. Even if it has the lowest prices and the most convenient shipping options. Adrian: If we, as consumers, want our shopping to have a positive impact, it's up to us Look for companies that are trying to make the world a better place. That could mean paying more for the things we buy, or it could mean buying less. The market-based society still has social goals. They just don't come from a central planner. Of course, some of our social preferences come from governments, but they also come from each of us and the decisions we make about what we do with our time, energy, and money. It's also important to remember that it's a privilege to be able to have these conversations. For many, many people around the world who live in poverty and struggle to afford the basic necessities of life, the ability to pay a high price based on conscience simply doesn't exist. Thanks for watching! See you next week. Crash Course in Economics was made possible by these wonderful people. You can support Crash Course on Patreon, a volunteer subscription system where your support helps keep Crash Course free for everyone, forever. And you'll get rewards too! Thanks for watching, and don't forget to be cool.

title: What are Incentives?
transcript: MRUniversity.com Learn Economics, Understand Your World Economics Glossary What is Incentive? What is encouragement? Incentives are rewards and punishments that motivate behavior. Incentives are everywhere. To better understand this critical economic concept, let's turn to the example of the British government hiring sea captains in 1787 to send convicts to Australia . The conditions on these ships were terrible. On one trip, more than a third of the men died, and the rest arrived beaten, hungry, and sick. The people were dissatisfied. Newspapers called for better conditions. Religious leaders appealed to the captains' sense of humanity, and the British Parliament passed laws demanding better treatment of these prisoners . Unfortunately, none of these attempts were successful. The death rate remained shockingly high. But at that time, there was an economist who proposed a new solution. Instead of paying captains for every prisoner who set sail for Australia, the government would only pay captains for prisoners who reached Australia alive . Overnight, the incentives of sea captains changed. The survival rate of prisoners reached 99%. As one observer put it, “ Economics has defeated feelings and kindness.” As you can see, incentives are a fundamental economic concept that helps us predict human behavior. But incentives are not the only fundamental concept. Marginal Revolution University Economics Dictionary
